we have distinguished between the two most recent examples cited, because in those instances we assume that certain adventitious <gloss>external</gloss> corpuscles are lodged within the body, which contribute to its firmness and enter into its constitution, even if perhaps only in a very small quantity. By contrast, we assume in this current case that these corpuscles do not materially combine to form the body upon which they act; instead, they merely agitate and variously move the particles composing it. This occurs perhaps by breaking some particles, bending and entangling others, and, to put it in a word, by changing the texture in such a way that those parts which were previously either moving separately or cohering less strictly are now reduced into a narrower space or a more intricate texture, and for this reason are more firmly connected to one another. 

That the bare arrangement of the parts of a body in relation to one another—without the addition of any extrinsic matter—can do much to produce stability, can be seen both in certain examples mentioned earlier and in willow twigs. When these twigs lie loose in a heap, they can each be easily separated from the rest; but when woven into a basket <note>Latin: "quasillum"</note>, they cohere so firmly that if one is lifted, all the others are raised with it. <summary>Boyle explains that firmness in bodies can result from a mere reorganization of their internal texture rather than the addition of new material. He uses the analogy of loose willow twigs versus a woven basket to illustrate how arrangement dictates stability.</summary>
